newsitem.title: FRANCE: Opposition leader slams France's Middle East "bias".
newsitem.headline: Opposition leader slams France's Middle East "bias".

text.p: The leader of France's opposition Socialists accused the conservative government on Sunday of bias against Israel and in favour of commercial and political interests in its conduct of Middle East policy.

"I do not want to talk about an 'Arab policy'," Socialist leader Lionel Jospin said in an interview, using the term used by many government officials to describe France's current approach to the Middle East.
"If France wants to play a role, it must continue to seek a balance and thus rely on its friendships and notably its friendship with Israel," Jospin told French Radio J.
Jospin's remarks were the opposition's harshest yet on foreign policy since conservative Jacques Chirac's election as French president in May 1995.

Chirac has avidly courted the region's Arab states and alienated many Israelis by pleading for a Palestinian state, the return of occupied Arab land to Syria and Lebanon and a bigger role for Europe -- and consequently a smaller role for Washington -- in the peace process.
During a visit to the region in October, he harshly and publicly criticised his Israeli guards while touring Jerusalem's old city.
French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette annoyed U.S. officials by launching a parallel diplomatic shuttle in the region last year at the same time as a U.S. initiative.
Critics have accused Paris of being motivated by a desire to boost its arms sales in the area while sewing up oil deals.

Jospin said French policy must be oriented towards "peace, democracy and co-development" and "must certainly not be motivated by afterthoughts about the presidential elections, or by commercial afterthoughts.

"Nor should we base our policy on cynicism or opportunism. We must conduct a policy that is based on principle and at the same time realistic," he told the radio station, which serves France's Jewish community.

De Charette, interviewed separately on the same station expressed France's satisfaction with the recent accord on Hebron between Israel and the Palestinian authority but said much remained to be done for peace in the region.

"We are involved (in the peace process), we are participating, we are going to continue to remain active -- the French, Europeans, Americans, all of us together, working towards a single goal," de Charette said.
